extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theology, ecclesiastical law, and clergy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts rules and normative principles about church power (excommunication, canonization, interpretation of Scripture, and ecclesiastical offices) and their relation to civil sovereignty from a historical/theological treatise. Focus is on when ecclesiastical acts are effective, who they bind, and what constitutes lawful church discipline and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of Judgment and Sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment (determination of merit) belongs to the Assembly of the faithful; the pronouncing of Sentence belongs always to the Apostle or some Pastor of the Church as Prolocutor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Matthew 18:18 and Paul's practice (1 Cor. 5:3-5): the Assembly first hears and judges the cause (especially when the Apostle is absent), and the Apostle or Pastor pronounceth the sentence. Example: Paul judged and pronounced sentence although he was absent in body, present in spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication is the part of the Power of the Keys by which men are thrust out from the Kingdom of God; originally Aposunagogon Poiein — 'to cast out of the Synagogue', i.e., out of the place of Divine service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term drawn from Jewish custom of casting out persons considered contagious in manners or doctrine (analogy to separation of lepers by Mosaic law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Excommunication when uncoupled from civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: When not strengthened by civil power, excommunication's use and effect was only that the faithful were to avoid the company of the excommunicated; it could not bar them from public places or compel civil exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 1 Cor. 5 and Matthew 18:17: believers should not 'keep company' or 'eat' with certain offending brethren, rendering them like 'a Heathen, and a Publican.' But excommunication did not prevent entry into places that belonged to civil dominion nor did it carry civil penalties absent civil enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication's limited effect upon apostates under persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: On a Christian who becomes an apostate in places where civil power persecutes or does not assist the Church, excommunication had no worldly damage nor terror; they return into favour of the world and are not in a worse estate in the world to come than those who never believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the effect relies on the believer's fear of exclusion from Christ's kingdom; apostates (unbelievers) are not sensible to such ecclesiastical punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication affects only the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication has effect only on those who believe Jesus will come again and expect admission into his Kingdom; it is a punishment relevant only to those who expect the coming judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Paul's phrase 'delivery to Satan' is explained: outside Christ's kingdom all kingdoms after judgment are 'in the Kingdom of Satan' — thus only the faithful fear the consequences of excommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication lies for injustice (Matthew 18 procedure) and for scandalous life (1 Cor. 5: fornicator, covetous, idolater, drunkard, extortioner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: private admonition, with witnesses, then before the Church; if unrepentant, treat as heathen/publican. Conversely, excommunication for mere difference of opinion that does not destroy the Christian foundation (belief that Jesus is the Christ) lacks scriptural authority and apostolic example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rejecting heretics and excommunicating
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts advising 'reject' or 'avoid' (e.g., Titus 3:10, 2 Tim. 2:23) are instructions to cease disputing or to 'set by' foolish questions, not commands to excommunicate fellow believers for disputed opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject (paraiteo) and avoid/periistaso in original language mean to give over admonishing or to avoid disputation; they are pastoral instructions, not prescriptions of disciplinary exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership and jurisdiction as prerequisites for Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is liable to excommunication only if he is a member of some lawful assembly (a Christian Church) that has the power to judge the cause for which excommunication is proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is no community or no power to judge, there can be no excommunication or sentence; the assembly deciding must be the lawful body constituted to judge such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Church cannot validly excommunicate another Church
rubrics_metrics.description: One Church cannot excommunicate another: either they are equal in power (in which case such a sentence is schism rather than discipline) or one is subordinate (in which case the part excommunicated ceases to be a Church and becomes a dissolute number of individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: excommunication presupposes an internal communal jurisdiction; inter-community excommunication is incoherent without a shared sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineffectiveness of Excommunication against sovereigns and their subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sovereign prince or assembly is excommunicated, the sentence is of no effect within his dominion: subjects are bound by nature to be in their sovereign's company/presence and cannot lawfully expel or refuse to eat with their sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, the excommunication of a Christian subject who obeys his own sovereign (whether Christian or heathen) is of no effect; true obedience to sovereign law supersedes ecclesiastical exclusion absent civil enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: True believer not liable to ecclesiastical harm from Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: One who truly believes Jesus is the Christ and has the Spirit of God dwelling in him can receive no harm by the excommunication of men; the real danger of excommunication concerns only those who believe in the coming kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus profession alone does not make one immune if hypocrisy in manners appears; external actions contrary to the sovereign's law are what the Church can judge in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family and subordinate relations not to be severed by another's Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Children and servants of an excommunicated parent or master are not forbidden to keep company with them or to eat with them; forbidding such would often deprive them of means and violate filial duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical pastoral consideration: imposing social prohibitions on dependents would cause greater injustice and contravene apostolic commands to honor parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Excommunication: correction of manners not coercive civil rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of excommunication, absent civil assistance, extends only to correcting manners (external behaviour) and to directing men toward salvation in the world to come, not to ruling by command and coercion in this world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a teacher may abandon an obstinate scholar (discipline) but has no ground to accuse him of injustice if the scholar was never obliged to obey; ecclesiastical authority is limited to teaching and admonition without civil force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter of Scripture in pre-Christian sovereign contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Before civil sovereigns became Christian, apostles (e.g., Paul at Thessalonica) preached and reasoned from Scriptures without legal commission; therefore those hearing were judges of the proof and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Gentiles did not already accept Jewish Scriptures, apostles used reason and testimony; no authoritative interpreter existed that converts were obliged to accept until civil authority created such an office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion does not confer legal force on Apostles' writings absent civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Apostolic writings were accepted by converts as true doctrine by faith, but did not become obligatory civil laws until lawful civil sovereigns commanded obedience to them; New Testament became law only where civil power made it so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law obliges only those who acknowledge the sovereign act; where civil power has not ordered obedience to apostolic writings, they remain authoritative counsel rather than binding legal commands in civil affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'Canonicall' — rule versus law
rubrics_metrics.description: A writing may be 'Canonicall' as a rule (a precept or guidance) in the sense of a teacher's counsel, but to be a law (obligatory canon) it must be prescribed by one whom the recipient is bound to obey — a sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes internal moral/pastoral authority (can be accepted by faith) from external legal obligation enforceable in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaic (Decalogue) laws became laws by the civil sovereign (Moses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ten Commandments and the Judicial and Levitical laws were made laws by Moses acting as civil sovereign; some parts are laws of nature (second table) and universally binding, others were particular statutes made law by the Israelite sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: a law obliges only to those who acknowledge the sovereign; Moses and subsequent high priests were the civil rulers who gave these commandments legal force in Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old Testament canonization tied to civil restoration under Esdras
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scriptures of the Old Testament were not universally canonical law for Jews until the restoration after the Captivity under Esdras; thereafter they were accepted as the Law of the Jews and made public (e.g., Greek translation by the Seventy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical status is connected to civil authority: Esdras as High Priest and civil sovereign confirmed the books' legal/religious authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils' decrees are persuasive counsel unless backed by civil sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of councils, including that of the Apostles (Acts 15), functioned as counsel and conditions proposed to converts and teachers, not as binding civil laws unless enforced by a lawful civil sovereign; 'to lay a burthen' in those contexts meant to propose conditions for salvation, not to create enforceable law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where councils 'lay a burden', the persons converted accepted these as conditions for salvation by faith; absent sovereign legislative power, such decrees cannot impose civil obligations or be disobeyed as sin in the civil sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on councils and later doctors to make Scripture law
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of councils or writings of doctors, assembled without civil sovereign authority, cannot make Scripture into law; the New Testament is law only where lawful civil power has made obedience to it obligatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: the earliest extant council collections (e.g., Laodicea) address ecclesiastical reading in churches (ecclesiastics) rather than imposing universal civil law; ecclesiastical mandates require civil sanction to become binding laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of ecclesiastical officers and criteria for Apostleship
rubrics_metrics.description: In apostolic times ecclesiastical officers were magisterial (preaching, administering sacraments, teaching) and ministerial (deacons administering secular necessities). Apostles were the principal magisterial officers chosen by Christ; essential mark of apostleship was being a witness of Christ's Resurrection (having seen him after the Resurrection or having conversed with him before).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: selection of a new apostle to replace Judas required that the candidate have the marks of apostolic witness; deacons were ministerial and concerned with temporal administration.
